system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2129-05-05 08:00:00 to 2129-05-14 12:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, bipolar disorder, PTSD, and prior alcohol abuse was admitted for acute on chronic pancreatitis due to two obstructing pancreatic duct stones causing ductal dilation. He presented with severe epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Pain was initially managed with IV Dilaudid and transitioned to PCA, then oral medications as symptoms improved. He advanced from sips to a low-fat diet, remained hemodynamically stable, and ambulated throughout the stay. Pre-operative workup including ECG and chest X-ray was completed, and he was discharged home in stable condition to prepare for an upcoming Puestow procedure. Discharge instructions included avoiding NSAIDs, continuing home medications, and follow-up with surgery and primary care.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

The specimen is reviewed for gross examination only by Dr. 
___.
 
Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the General Surgical Service on 
___ for further surgical intervention of the aforementioned 
problem.  On that date, the patient underwent Puestow procedure 
with Roux-en-Y formation and intraoperative ultrasound, which 
went well without complication (reader referred to the Operative 
Note for details). After a brief, uneventful stay in the PACU, 
the patient arrived on the floor NPO with an NG tube, on IV 
fluids, with a foley catheter in place, and a Dilaudid PCA for 
pain control.  The patient was hemodynamically stable.
.
Hospital course notable for episodic confusion and a single 
seizure-like episode on POD#7. Both Neurology and Psychiatry 
were consulted; their recommendations appreciated. Neurology 
felt that his ""seizure-like"" episode was nonepileptic and 
similar to those in the past, which had been fully evaluated, 
and that further investigation would not be necessary. The 
patient did not expereince any subsequent episodes, and remained 
on his anti-seizure regimen. Psychiatry felt that his early 
episodes of confusion were mostlikely due to his post-operative 
narcotic regimen. The regimen was progressively weaned with 
resolution of the confusion. He was cleared for discharge.
.

Dilaudid PCA and IV Toradol alone. On POD#1, Methadone 10mg IV 
TID was added with improved pain control. When the patient was 
able to tolerate a clear diet, IV Methadone was converted to 
oral formulation. The Chronic Pain Service was consulted to 
assist with tapering the patient off Methadone, and further 
conversion to an oral regimen. To aid with the conversion, he 
was placed on Gabapentin and Tizanidine along with Dilaudid PO 
PRN with continued good pain control. The NG tube was 
discontinued on POD#3, and  the patient was started on sips of 
clears on POD#3. Diet was progressively advanced as tolerated to 
a regular diet by POD#7.  The foley catheter was discontinued 
the morning of POD#3. The patient subsequently voided without 
problem. 
.
During this hospitalization, the patient ambulated early and 
frequently, was adherent with respiratory toilet and incentive 
spirrometry, and actively participated in the plan of care. The 
patient received subcutaneous heparin and venodyne boots were 
used during this stay. The patient's blood sugar was monitored 
regularly throughout the stay; sliding scale insulin was 
administered when indicated. Labwork was routinely followed; 
electrolytes were repleted when indicated. Given his history of 
seizures, seizure precautions were maintained throughout his 
stay.
.
At the time of discharge, the patient was doing well, afebrile 
with stable vital signs. The patient was tolerating a regular 
diet, ambulating, voiding without assistance, and pain was well 
controlled on Dilaudid PO PRN and a Gabapentin taper. He was 
discharged home with ___ services. The patient received 
discharge teaching and follow-up instructions with understanding 
verbalized and agreement with the discharge plan.

radiology_notes.text:
INTRAOPERATIVE ULTRASOUND OF THE PANCREAS

CLINICAL INDICATION:  Chronic pancreatitis with pancreatic duct obstruction,
to facilitate for Puestow drainage procedure.

High-resolution linear array scans were performed directly on the pancreatic
surface demonstrating a markedly dilated pancreatic duct measuring up to 7 mm
in diameter.  In the pancreatic neck, a large 8 x 10 mm stone is seen
obstructing the pancreatic duct.  The duct is clear in the body, but as scans
extended toward the pancreatic tail another large intraluminal stone of
approximately 10 mm is seen within the duct.  In addition to this, there are
numerous coarse calcifications and smaller stones in the pancreatic parenchyma
and in side branch ducts.

Under real-time guidance, a 21-gauge needle was positioned into the dilated
pancreatic duct in the body of the gland, and this was used as a localizing
device to guide incision of the pancreas down into the dilated pancreatic duct
for purposes of surgical drainage.

CONCLUSION:  Chronic pancreatitis with calcifications and stones obstructing
the pancreatic duct.  Successful needle localization of the duct was performed
followed by surgical incision of the duct and subsequent drainage procedure.

HISTORY:  Line placement.

FINDINGS:  In comparison with the study of ___, there has been placement of a
right IJ catheter that extends to the mid portion of the SVC.  Nasogastric
tube extends well into the stomach.  Cardiac silhouette remains within normal
limits.  No definite acute pneumonia or vascular congestion or pleural
effusion.

EXAM:  Abdominal radiograph obtained ___.

___.

HISTORY:  Abdominal pain.

TECHNIQUE:  Supine portable radiograph of the abdomen were obtained.

FINDINGS:

Multiple soft tissue staples are noted over the midline abdomen.  Right upper
quadrant cholecystectomy clips are identified.  There is an NG tube with its
tip in the stomach.  Multiple lines overlie the abdomen, likely external to
the patient.

Dilated loops of small and large bowel are noted throughout the abdomen with
bowel gas noted to the level of the rectum.   Supine technique limits
evaluation for air-fluid levels and free intraperitoneal air.  No suspicious
calcifications are noted within the abdomen or pelvis.

Osseous structures are grossly unremarkable in appearance.

IMPRESSION:

Limited portable radiograph of the abdomen demonstrate dilated loops of bowel
throughout the abdomen to the level of the rectum.  These findings are most
likely related to an ileus.

AP CHEST, 6:31 P.M. ON ___

HISTORY:  Acute change in respiratory status.  Abdominal pain.  Question
pneumothorax or perforation.

IMPRESSION:
AP chest compared to ___:

Right jugular line ends at the superior cavoatrial junction.  Elevation of the
right lung base has increased, but there is no appreciable right pleural
effusion, no pneumothorax or pneumoperitoneum.  Aside from mild infrahilar
atelectasis lungs are clear.  Heart size is normal.

INDICATION:  Patient is a ___ male with tachycardia and desaturation
on ambulation.  Evaluate for pulmonary embolism.

EXAMINATION:  CT of the torso with intravenous contrast.

COMPARISONS:  Comparison is made to examination from ___ and radiographs
from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Helically-acquired axial images were obtained from the thoracic
inlet to the mid abdomen initially without the administration of intravenous
contrast and after the administration of both 130 cc and 170 cc of Optiray 350
intravenous contrast.  A repeat examination was performed because original
series was nondiagnostic for pulmonary embolism.  Coronal, sagittal, and
oblique reformations were obtained.  Subsequently, helically-acquired axial
images were obtained from the lung bases to the pubic symphysis after the
administration of both oral and intravenous contrast using a CT enterography
protocol.  Coronal and sagittal reformations were obtained.

FINDINGS:

CT OF THE CHEST WITH AND WITHOUT INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  There is a 26 x 25 mm
right hilar lymph node/mass.  No other significant adenopathy with scattered
axillary and mediastinal lymph nodes not meeting size criteria for pathologic
enlargement.  No left hilar adenopathy.  Atherosclerotic calcification is
noted within the coronary arteries and the thoracic aorta.  The heart and
great vessels are, otherwise, unremarkable.  There is no evidence pericardial
effusion.

There are multiple scattered areas of ground-glass opacification with an upper
lobe predominance that is nonspecific and could relate to infectious or
inflammatory etiologies.  In addition, there is right basilar patchy
opacification with either mucus/aspirated material seen within the right lower
lobe segmental bronchi that in this setting is concerning for aspiration.  No
discrete pulmonary nodules are noted.  There is no evidence of pleural
effusions.

There is no evidence of acute aortic syndrome.  There is no evidence of
pulmonary embolism to the subsegmental levels.

CT OF THE ABDOMEN WITH INTRAVENOUS AND ORAL CONTRAST:  Patient is noted to be
status post cholecystectomy.  The patient is also noted to be status post
recent Puestow procedure with side-to-side anastomosis of the pancreatic body
with the jejunum.  There is post-surgical change with stranding noted about
this region and a single focus of free air within the abdomen (3B:119) within
expected postoperative change.  The liver, spleen, both adrenal glands, both
kidneys, and both ureters are unremarkable.  Visualized portions of
intra-abdominal small and large bowel are unremarkable other than postsurgical
changes described above.  There is no discrete fluid collection concerning for
abscess.  There is no extraluminal contrast noted to suggest leak.  There are
extensive calcifications noted throughout the pancreas compatible with known
history of chronic pancreatitis.  Scattered mesenteric lymph nodes and
retroperitoneal lymph nodes do not meet size criteria for pathologic
enlargement, likely reactive in nature.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITH INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  The rectum, sigmoid colon,
bladder, prostate, and seminal vesicles are unremarkable.  There is no pelvic
free fluid.  There is no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

BONE WINDOWS:  The visualized osseous structures are unremarkable and no
suspicious lytic or sclerotic foci identified.

IMPRESSION:
1.  New scattered ground-glass opacification with upper lobe predominance,
nonspecific, could be related to infectious or inflammatory etiologies.

2.  2.5 x 2.6 cm right hilar lymph node/mass.  Differential includes neoplasm
or may be reactive in nature, recommend bronchoscopy to exclude neoplasm.

3.  Expected post-surgical change status post Puestow procedure.  Extensive
pancreatic calcifications compatible with known chronic pancreatitis.

4.  Likely right lower lobe aspiration.

Findings were discussed with Dr. ___ at 2:30 p.m. on ___.

diagnoses.long_title: Other opiates and related narcotics causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You're here today for your Puestow procedure to help with your chronic pancreatitis pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve been having a lot of pain lately, especially in the middle of my belly. Is this surgery going to fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the goal is to relieve the pain. We found that your main pancreatic duct is blocked by stones and is dilated. The Puestow procedure will open and drain that duct, which should reduce the pressure and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember having stones before. They took them out with a scope, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. You’ve had several ERCPs in the past. But now the blockage is more extensive, and the duct is permanently narrowed. Surgery is the best option now to create a long-term drainage path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Will I be asleep the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be under general anesthesia. The surgery usually takes a few hours. We’ll also use an intraoperative ultrasound to help locate the duct and stones precisely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sounds good. I’m ready to get this done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, it’s Dr. Lee again. The surgery went very well. We performed the Puestow with a Roux-en-Y drainage and used ultrasound to guide us. We removed two large stones from your pancreatic duct.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I feel groggy, but no pain yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a Dilaudid PCA pump for pain, so you can control it as needed. You have an NG tube to rest your stomach and a catheter for urine. We’ll remove those as you recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be on the NG tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually a few days. Once your bowel starts working again, we’ll remove it and start you on small sips of water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your white count is high, which is expected after surgery. Your kidney function is stable, and we’re managing your blood sugar with insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a little foggy. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from the pain meds. We’re watching that. We’re also giving you heparin shots and compression boots to prevent clots, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember I had a DVT before. Glad you’re on top of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding methadone to your pain regimen because the Dilaudid alone wasn’t enough. It’s stronger and longer-lasting, which should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is methadone safe? I’ve heard it’s for addiction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s used for addiction, but also for severe pain. We’ll use it short-term and taper it as you heal. The Chronic Pain Service will help manage the transition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news — your NG tube is out. You can start with small sips of clear liquids. We’ll advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m starving. Can I have broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, clear broth is perfect. We’ll see how you tolerate it and move to soft foods tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s already out. You’ve been able to urinate on your own, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray shows some dilated bowel loops. This is common after surgery — it’s called an ileus. It means your gut is still waking up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. We’re encouraging you to walk and use the incentive spirometer to help everything get moving. It should resolve in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan because you had some trouble breathing when walking. It shows some fluid in your lungs, likely from aspiration, and a lymph node in your chest we need to check out later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Aspiration? How did that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes after surgery, especially with sedation, stomach contents can go into the lungs. It’s not uncommon. We’ll monitor it and make sure it clears.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lymph node?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be reactive from infection or inflammation. But we recommend a bronchoscopy later to rule out anything serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a brief episode yesterday that looked like a seizure. Neurology was consulted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember that. Was it a real seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology thinks it was a nonepileptic event, similar to pseudoseizures you’ve had before. They don’t recommend more testing. Psychiatry thinks the confusion was from the narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my epilepsy acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’re still on your seizure meds, but this wasn’t a true seizure. We’re tapering the narcotics, and your mental clarity has improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel much more like myself today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’re on a regular diet, walking without help, and your pain is controlled with oral hydromorphone and gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll send you home with pain meds, Viokase for digestion, and a nicotine patch since you’re trying to quit smoking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume all your home medications — lisinopril, simvastatin, ziprasidone, omeprazole, and the others — unless we say otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take it at bedtime for four days to help with nerve pain and then stop. We’re also giving you a short supply of hydromorphone for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: You’ll be discharged tomorrow morning. A home health nurse will check on you, and you’ll follow up with me and your PCP in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you have increasing pain, redness or drainage from the incision, fever, or trouble breathing. No heavy lifting for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can shower. Gently wash the area and pat it dry. No baths or swimming until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not while on pain meds. Wait until you’re off them and cleared by your surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll take it slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. You’re alert, eating well, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember to rest, keep walking, and follow up with your doctors. The home health nurse will visit tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And I’ll schedule the bronchoscopy soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Take care, and call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Meds, diet, incision care, follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve done great this week. Healing takes time, but you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a lot better already. Hope the pain keeps improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will. We’ll adjust your pain plan as needed. Don’t hesitate to call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one more thing — should I keep taking the nicotine patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use it daily as prescribed. It can help with cravings. Let your PCP know how it’s going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’m really trying to quit this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Support is available if you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you understand when to take your meds and when to call us?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, hydromorphone only if needed, gabapentin at night for four days, and call if I have fever or wound issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And no NSAIDs — stick to acetaminophen if you need extra pain relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No ibuprofen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve got a good grasp on everything. We’re confident you’ll do well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, the nurse said I can leave soon. Just wanted to say goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with chronic pancreatitis, bipolar disorder, PTSD, and a history of alcohol abuse was admitted for a Puestow procedure due to obstructing pancreatic duct stones causing ductal dilation and severe pain. He underwent successful surgery with Roux-en-Y drainage and intraoperative ultrasound guidance. Post-operatively, he experienced inadequate pain control initially, which was managed by adding methadone and later transitioning to oral hydromorphone and gabapentin. He developed transient confusion and a single nonepileptic seizure-like episode on post-operative day 7, attributed to narcotics and managed with dose tapering. His diet advanced from NPO to regular, and he ambulated early. A CT scan revealed a right hilar lymph node requiring bronchoscopy and findings suggestive of aspiration. He was discharged home with home health services, on a regimen including pain medication, Viokase, and a nicotine patch, with follow-up planned with surgery and primary care.
